newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke blames splits, sleaze for defeat.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke blames splits, sleaze for defeat.

text.p: Kenneth Clarke, favourite to take over the leadership of Britain's battered Conservatives, on Thursday blamed party divisions and so-called sleaze for their election defeat.
The former finance minister also made a veiled attack on John Major, ousted as prime minister by Labour's landslide election victory on May 1, promising tougher leadership if he took over from Major.

Clarke, in an interview with the right-wing Spectator magazine, said the Conservative party lost power after 18 years in office because voters became fed up with "interminable internal debate and sleaze". Senior Conservatives were the subject of allegations about financial and sexual misdemeanours in the run-up to the election.
In a remark immediately interpreted as a shot at Major, Clarke said it was a lack of strong leadership which allowed debate to run out of hand and lost the election.
"(Labour campaign chief) Peter Mandelson didn't win, the government lost. Labour exploited our mistakes. Against a strong Government that would not have been adequate," said Clarke.
Clarke, a feisty and colourful politician on the left of the party, is among his party's finest parliamentary performers and was conspicuously loyal to Major in the dying days of his government.
Nominations for the leadership battle's first round closed on Thursday, leaving Clarke facing four more former cabinet ministers in the first round on June 10.
On Wednesday Clarke received the backing of former health secretary Stephen Dorrell who pulled out of the race himself.

Second favourite is former Welsh Secretary William Hague, 36. The other candidates are former interior minister Michael Howard, former social security secretary Peter Lilley and former Welsh secretary John Redwood.

But the complicated rules for selecting the party leader -- likely to be changed after the current contest following criticism they do not give rank and file party members a say -- mean the final outcome is open.

The only people entitled to vote are the party's 164 members of parliament. The winner in the first ballot needs an overall majority of the Conservative members of parliament plus a lead of 15 percent over his nearest rival.

In the second round on June 17, the winner needs a straight majority. But if no one succeeds --- and an outright winner is not expected in the second round -- the top two candidates go through to a straight fight on June 19.
The arcane nature of the election makes the outcome extremely hard to forecast, with MPs often switching allegiances between one round of voting and the next.

Margaret Thatcher, who beat Edward Heath in 1975 and went on to become one of the most prominent British prime ministers of the 20th century, was not initially thought likely to win the party leadership.
Thatcher was ousted herself in a leadership battle in 1990 when Major took over as leader and prime minister.
